title: Cavity Enhanced Superconductivity
authors: Hanxiang Zhang, Zexin Feng, I-Te Lu, Zhiwei Li, Songhao Guo, Qiuyu Shang, Dening Luan, Mingcheng Panmai, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Angel Rubio, Weibo Gao
abstract: Vacuum electromagnetic fluctuations have recently emerged as a promising means of controlling collective quantum phases. Although cavity-induced modifications of superconductivity have been widely predicted, experimental studies have so far reported only suppression of superconducting properties. Here, by carefully tuning a terahertz cavity to resonate with key phononic modes in few-layer niobium diselenide (NbSe2), we demonstrate cavity-enhanced superconductivity in few-layer NbSe2 coupled to a complementary split-ring resonator. In trilayer NbSe2, the superconducting transition temperature increases by ~10%, from 3.02 K to 3.41 K, when coupled to a cavity resonant at 2.04 THz. The enhancement exhibits a clear spatial dependence following the cavity field profile and a non-monotonic frequency dependence, with maximal enhancement near 2 THz. These results provide experimental evidence that vacuum electromagnetic fields can enhance superconductivity and establish cavity engineering as a powerful platform for tailoring quantum materials.
summary: The authors experimentally demonstrate that coupling a superconductor ($	ext{NbSe}_2$) to an engineered terahertz cavity (CSRR) can enhance its critical temperature. By tuning the cavity resonance near $2 	ext{ THz}$, they achieved up to a 10% increase in $T_c$, establishing cavity engineering as a powerful tool for tailoring quantum materials.
main_problem: To experimentally demonstrate that vacuum electromagnetic fluctuations, controlled via cavity engineering, can enhance superconductivity in quantum materials.
main_result: The superconducting transition temperature ($T_{c,0}$) of few-layer $	ext{NbSe}_2$ increased by approximately 10% when coupled to a terahertz cavity resonant at $2.04 	ext{ THz}$.
method: Transport measurements (R-T curves) were performed on superconducting films integrated with a complementary split-ring resonator (CSRR) structure, combined with field simulations.
model_or_system: The system involves few-layer niobium diselenide ($	ext{NbSe}_2$), a van der Waals superconductor, coupled to a $	ext{THz}$ cavity formed by a CSRR. The study probes the interaction between superconductivity and local electromagnetic fields.
key_observables: Superconducting transition temperature ($T_{c,0}$), lower critical field ($H_{c1}$), and the change in $T_{c,0}$ ($\Delta T_c$).
important_parameters: Resonant frequency of the cavity (e.g., $2.04 	ext{ THz}$), local electric field strength ($\sim 0.8 	ext{ V/m}$), and material thickness.
main_assumptions: The enhancement is attributed to the resonant electromagnetic environment, after rigorously ruling out contributions from sample inhomogeneity or charge density wave (CDW) effects via control experiments.
figures_summary: Figures show $R$-$T$ curves demonstrating enhanced $T_{c,0}$ at specific cavity resonances ($2.04 	ext{ THz}$) compared to baseline measurements, and plots illustrating the spatial dependence of this enhancement across the cavity field profile.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by noting previous suppression results, then presents the experimental setup using $	ext{NbSe}_2$/CSRR. It systematically measures $T_{c,0}$ as a function of location (spatial mapping) and resonance frequency (spectral mapping), concluding that optimal enhancement occurs near $2 	ext{ THz}$.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges cavity quantum electrodynamics principles into condensed matter physics by using engineered electromagnetic environments to tune fundamental superconducting properties, which is highly relevant for open quantum systems research.
